citeAs: Pan Lu, Hritik Bansal, Tony Xia, Jiacheng Liu, Chunyuan Li, Hannaneh Hajishirzi, Hao Cheng, Kai-Wei Chang, Michel Galley, Jianfeng Gao (2024). MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts. ICLR 2024.
creator: Pan Lu, Hritik Bansal, Tony Xia, Jiacheng Liu, Chunyuan Li, Hannaneh Hajishirzi, Hao Cheng, Kai-Wei Chang, Michel Galley, Jianfeng Gao (UCLA, University of Washington, Microsoft Research)
description: MathVista is a benchmark for evaluating mathematical reasoning of foundation models in visual contexts. It consists of 6,141 examples derived from 28 existing multimodal datasets involving mathematics and 3 newly created datasets (IQTest, FunctionQA, and PaperQA), covering seven types of mathematical reasoning and diverse visual contexts including geometry diagrams, charts, natural images, and more.
name: MathVista
publisher: UCLA, University of Washington, Microsoft Research
rai:annotationsPerItem: 3 (three expert annotators per item for VQA mathematical reasoning labeling; three reviewers per item for new dataset annotation)
rai:annotatorDemographics: New dataset annotators were graduate students in STEM fields. Human performance evaluators on Amazon Mechanical Turk were required to have a high school diploma or higher, a history of completing more than 5,000 HIT tasks, and an acceptance score higher than 0.99.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Inter-annotation consistency rate of 99.2% for the newly collected 736 questions (only 6 exhibited disagreements). For VQA mathematical reasoning labeling, a Fleiss Kappa score of 0.775 was achieved among three annotators, indicating substantial agreement. For automatic mathematical reasoning category annotation, 94.1% of examples had the exact same set of reasoning types between automatic and human annotations, while 98.79% of individual labels were identical.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Custom annotation tool (GUI shown in paper figures) for dataset annotation; Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) for human performance evaluation and Bard assessment task
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Three expert annotators manually labeled VQA examples to determine if they involve mathematical reasoning, using majority voting. For the three new datasets, all questions were manually annotated by graduate students in STEM fields and refined through a rigorous review process. Each dataset was independently annotated by three reviewers, with discrepancies resolved through discussion. For mathematical reasoning category labeling, expert annotators manually labeled 1,000 examples from seven candidates using an annotation tool.
rai:dataCollection: MathVista was collected from three sources: (1) nine MathQA datasets in multimodal settings (2,666 examples), (2) 19 VQA datasets selected from over 70 reviewed datasets containing math-related instances (2,739 examples), and (3) three newly created datasets (IQTest, FunctionQA, PaperQA) with 736 newly curated examples. Each source dataset was limited to up to 400 examples to ensure balanced representation.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consists of 28 existing multimodal datasets (9 MathQA datasets and 19 VQA datasets) plus three newly created datasets. Source datasets include geometry problem solving datasets, math word problem datasets, textbook QA datasets, figure QA datasets, and general VQA datasets covering diverse visual contexts.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping
rai:dataLimitations: Dataset coverage may have gaps in certain types of mathematical problems and visuals. Only 85.6% of examples have annotations due to sourcing from original data providers. Annotations lack a unified format and structure due to heterogeneity of sources. The benchmark focuses on specific domains (science and college-level math), limiting scalability and generalizability to other domains. The study focused exclusively on the most recent and prominent models.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Each source dataset was limited to up to 400 examples to ensure balanced representation. For testmini sampling: (1) randomly sample questions with a threshold number of 4 for each source dataset; (2) randomly sample remaining questions for each source dataset proportional to its representation in the entire set. The KL Divergence between testmini and the entire set is 0.008 and Total Variation distance is 0.035.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For VQA datasets, heuristic rules were used to automatically select examples likely to involve mathematical reasoning: examples with numeric answers or those containing quantity words were selected. This automatic filtration yielded 4,949 VQA-format examples. Coarse labels of mathematical reasoning were automatically obtained from source dataset details. Metadata including question type, answer type, language, source, category, task, grade level, and visual context were annotated.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The answer labels for the test set will not be publicly released to prevent data contamination; an online evaluation platform will be maintained. The authors are committed to maintaining the datasets (e.g., refining potential data noise) in response to community feedback, and to evolving the leaderboard in response to new models.
rai:dataSocialImpact: MathVista is intended to drive development of general-purpose AI agents capable of tackling mathematically intensive and visually rich real-world tasks, with applications in educational disciplines, logical queries about statistical data, and theorem proving and scientific discovery in advanced research fields.
rai:dataUseCases: Evaluating mathematical reasoning capabilities of LLMs and LMMs in visual contexts; benchmarking foundation models on tasks requiring fine-grained visual understanding and compositional reasoning; facilitating development of mathematical reasoning systems in visually intensive scenarios; model development validation (testmini subset).
rai:machineAnnotationTools: GPT-4 (used as answer extractor with >99.5% accuracy on 200 examples); EasyOCR (used for OCR text detection in augmented LLM experiments); Multimodal Bard (used for image caption generation in augmented LLM experiments)

null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: No specific timeframe for data collection is mentioned in the paper, except that PaperQA sourced papers released in August 2023.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: No discussion of missing data handling in the collection process; the 85.6% annotation coverage is noted as a limitation but no imputation or gap-filling is described.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol is described in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: No personal or sensitive information is collected; the dataset consists of mathematical reasoning questions with images.
null_reasons.rai:dataBiases: No explicit bias acknowledgements or bias mitigation design decisions are discussed in the paper beyond general limitations.

evidence.name: we present MATHVISTA, a benchmark designed to combine challenges from diverse mathematical and visual tasks.
evidence.description: It consists of 6,141 examples, derived from 28 existing multimodal datasets involving mathematics and 3 newly created datasets (i.e., IQTest, FunctionQA, and PaperQA). Completing these tasks requires fine-grained, deep visual understanding and compositional reasoning, which all state-of-the-art foundation models find challenging.

evidence.isLiveDataset: MATHVISTA consists of 6,141 examples, divided into two subsets: testmini and test. testmini contains 1,000 examples, intended for model development validation or for those with limited computing resources. The testset features the remaining 5,141 examples for standard evaluation.
evidence.rai:dataCollection: We collected nine MathQA datasets in multimodal settings, including four for GPS, two for MWP with visual contexts of synthetic scenes, abstract diagrams, and tables, and two for TQA on college curricula. Each source dataset is limited to up to 400 examples to ensure a balanced representation of each source in our final compiled benchmark. In total, we collected 2,666 examples.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionType: We reviewed more than 70 datasets, collecting 19 of them that contain math-related instances and are publicly available. IQTest comprises 228 examples requiring inductive reasoning, abstract thinking, pattern prediction, and calculations, sourced from puzzle test figures on online learning platforms.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: MATHVISTA incorporates 28 existing multimodal datasets, including 9 math-targeted question answering (MathQA) datasets and 19 VQA datasets. In addition, we have created three new datasets (i.e., IQTest, FunctionQA, PaperQA) which are tailored to evaluating logical reasoning on puzzle test figures, algebraic reasoning over functional plots, and scientific reasoning with academic paper figures, respectively.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: we initially designed heuristic rules to automatically select examples likely to involve mathematical reasoning from a large pool of candidates. Examples with numeric answers or those containing quantity words (as listed in §D.1) in the questions were selected. This automatic filtration yielded 4,949 VQA-format examples, though some false positive examples remained.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: we engaged three expert annotators to manually label these examples to determine if they involve mathematical reasoning. To ensure data quality, all questions were manually annotated by graduate students in STEM fields and further refined through a rigorous review process. To ensure consistency in annotation, we employed a two-step process. Initially, each dataset was independently annotated by three reviewers, resulting in a high inter-annotation consistency rate of 99.2%.
evidence.rai:annotationsPerItem: we engaged three expert annotators to manually label these examples to determine if they involve mathematical reasoning. Initially, each dataset was independently annotated by three reviewers, resulting in a high inter-annotation consistency rate of 99.2%.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Initially, each dataset was independently annotated by three reviewers, resulting in a high inter-annotation consistency rate of 99.2%. Specifically, among the newly collected 736 questions, only 6 exhibited disagreements in the annotated answers. Our analysis yielded a Fleiss Kappa score of 0.775, indicating a substantial level of consistency among the annotators.
evidence.rai:annotatorDemographics: To ensure data quality, all questions were manually annotated by graduate students in STEM fields and further refined through a rigorous review process. Each question from the testmini subset was assigned to five annotators, all of whom have a history of completing more than 5,000 HIT tasks and boast an acceptance score higher than 0.99.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: We developed an annotation tool, as illustrated in Figure 22, to enable expert annotators to label problems that involve mathematical reasoning. We conducted a study to evaluate human performance on the testmini subset of the MATHVISTA, utilizing Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT).
evidence.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: we adopted this sampling strategy: (1) first, randomly sample questions with a threshold number of 4 for each source dataset; (2) then, randomly sample the remaining questions for each source dataset on its proportion in the entire set. The KL Divergence and Total Variation (TV) distance between the testmini set and the entire set are 0.008 and 0.035, respectively
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: One limitation is the dataset coverage. While MATHVISTA encompasses a broad spectrum of tasks and visual contexts, there may be gaps in the representation of certain types of mathematical problems and visuals. Annotations were sourced from original data providers, resulting in only 85.6% of examples (Table 1) having annotations. Due to the heterogeneity of these sources, annotations lack a unified format and structure.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: it is essential to develop a new benchmark to (1) facilitate the development of mathematical reasoning systems in visually intensive scenarios, and (2) evaluate the research progress of LLMs and LMMs, especially their capabilities in solving rigorous reasoning tasks.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: This significant gap underscores the critical role that MATHVISTA will play in the development of general-purpose AI agents capable of tackling mathematically intensive and visually rich real-world tasks.
evidence.rai:machineAnnotationTools: We propose an answer extractor (§F.2) based on LLMs such as GPT-4, inspired by its remarkable ability for text processing. A preliminary study of 200 examples shows that GPT-4 can extract the answer text with more than 99.5% accuracy.
evidence.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: the answer labels for test will not be publicly released to prevent data contamination, and we will maintain an online evaluation platform. Our benchmark is part of an ongoing research process, and we are committed to maintaining the datasets, such as refining the potential data noise, in response to the community feedback. Also, we are committed to evolving the leaderboard in response to new models.
